summary: The note describes a growing U.S. movement of livestock and poultry farmers who use local feed, sustainable practices and ethical rearing to produce meats with distinct regional flavors. It profiles farmers in several states, cites UC Davis research on how diet and stress affect flavor, and covers challenges such as year-round feed supply. It also notes strong consumer demand and planned educational workshops for the latter half of 2024.
one_line: Farmers across the U.S. are using local feed and sustainable rearing to create regionally distinctive meat and poultry flavors, backed by research and consumer demand.
key_facts: Since September 2023, a growing number of U.S. livestock and poultry farmers have been exploring how local feed affects their animals' meat.

Sarah Jacobs, a fourth-generation cattle rancher in Montana, says her ranch has seen an improved beef flavor profile since switching to local feed of indigenous grasses, barley and other crops; the ranch has operated since October 2023.
George Thompson, a poultry farmer in Oregon who started his venture in early 2024, says the local grains he uses are rich in omega-3s and give his poultry a richer, more nuanced flavor.

Elaine Marshall in Virginia began raising heritage pigs after September 2023, feeding them acorns, hickory nuts and apples from local woods and orchards, which gives the pork a slightly sweet, complex profile.
Carlos Mendez runs a family-owned sheep farm in New Mexico and adopted rotational grazing in late 2023, noticing a marked improvement in the flavor of his lamb.
Carlos Mendez's sheep graze on local grasses, herbs and clovers rotated seasonally, so the land is not overused and the diet stays diverse.

Dr. Amelia Richards at the University of California, Davis, began a study in January 2023 on how an animal's diet influences the final flavor of meat; she cites fatty acids, amino acids and carotenoids as factors.
Dr. Richards' study emphasizes that animal stress levels, shaped by living conditions and treatment, affect muscle development and fat distribution, and thus flavor.
Jason Bennett, a Colorado rancher, says sourcing enough local feed year-round is hard, especially in harsh winters.
Vertical farming and hydroponics for feed production are on the rise, and farmers are pursuing collaborative arrangements to ensure steady year-round local feed supply.

Meats from regional producers sell out of farmers' markets and specialty butchers faster than ever; Chicago chef Marsha Clemens says patrons rave about the taste and come back for the authentic flavor.
Workshops, webinars and resource materials are planned for the latter half of 2024, led by the Farm-To-Table Cooperative and the Sustainable Farming Institute.
